newsitem.title: JAPAN: Asia currency woes hurt region's oil product trade.
newsitem.headline: Asia currency woes hurt region's oil product trade.

text.p: This year's rash of Asian currency crises comes at a bad time for the region's oil product markets, dampening demand just as new production from ongoing refinery expansion has raised supplies, energy analysts say.

Refinery additions, expected to add some 2.8 million barrels per day (bpd) to Asia's overall refining capacity by 2000, had just begun to gather speed when widespread currency woes affecting Malaysia, the Philippines, Thailand, and most recently Indonesia hit the region's ability to absorb the growing supplies.
Inventories of middle distillates in the Asian trade centre of Singapore last week were a massive 40 percent above year-earlier levels at 10.23 million barrels.

Analysts say new capacity additions during 1996 of 620,000 bpd in South Korea and 275,000 bpd in Thailand are largely responsible for the rise, although short-term factors such as lower Chinese diesel buying and a first-quarter importing spree by independent Singapore traders are also to blame.

Growth in Asian oil product demand, meanwhile, has slowed dramatically in pace-setting economies such as Thailand and South Korea, with demand figures from Indonesia, Malaysia and the Philippines faring little better, analysts say.

Thailand, which has suffered a 20 percent drop in the value of its currency since July 2, was already on shaky demand footing, having logged a 1.2 percent decline in oil product demand for the first half of 1997.

Although refinery construction has been slowed to some extent by the currency crunch, a 300,000 bpd climb in Asian crude distillation capacity is still expected by the end of this year, according to data from Washington's Petroleum Finance Company (PFC).

"The timing is not at all ideal for the region to be experiencing a product surplus, given the economic slowdown we've seen," said Sara Banaszak, an analyst with the Honolulu based East-West Energy Center.

Hardest hit in the near term will be refinery profit margins, as product prices decline against stable crude demand, although traders note that the potential arrival of newly exported Iraqi crude volumes into Asia could provide some relief by pushing crude prices lower.

"The outlook has been pretty dismal for margins, given how saturated Asian product markets are, but crude prices could give refiners a break if a lot of Iraqi barrels start heading this way," said a trader with a Japanese refiner.
Iraq began exporting crude oil to world markets last week in the second phase of sales allowed under United Nations resolution 986.

Indonesia, whose currency is also under pressure, still hopes for an additional 250,000 bpd of capacity on top of its existing 989,500 bpd and last week laid down measures aimed at facilitating private investment in new plants.

China has banned all new refinery construction until 2000 but will focus on expansion at existing sites, while India's planned increases will probably be delayed by restrictions on foreign capital investment.
China's Zhenhai Refining & Chemical Co Ltd said on Monday it had completed part of a project to expand its refining capacity by 8.0 million tonnes per year (138,000 bpd).
Vietnam, which had vowed to start work this year on a 130,000 bpd facility called Dung Quat in a remote coastal region, is still scrambling to cover the plant's projected $1.5 billion cost.

"Vietnam had hopes of generating growth in the north of the country with Dung Quat, but many outside observers consider the plant's location unfeasible," said analyst Craig Pennington with UBS Securities Ltd in Tokyo.
Pennington added that in the medium term a slowdown in refinery expansion would begin to benefit Asia's existing refiners.
He said: "We're not expecting a rampant recovery in refinery margins, but a slowdown in new builds leaves definite scope for improvement over the next few years."
